title: Lech Lecha: not a thread (Genesis 14:22–23)
hookLine: Abram refuses the spoils of Sodom, not even a thread or a shoe-latchet

cards: Someone offers you something you didn't quite earn. A gift from a person who'll want a favor later. Credit for a project someone else mostly did.
A discount you know is a mistake. It's right there, taking it would be easy, and nobody would really blame anyone for it. In the middle of Lech Lecha, Abram is offered a whole city's wealth.
He did win it, in battle. The king himself tells him to keep it. Here's what he says instead.

teach.h: ABRAM RESCUES LOT AND THE GOODS.
teach.b: Four kings make war on five kings, including the king of Sodom. Sodom loses. The victors carry off its people and its goods, and among the captives is Abram's nephew Lot.
Abram hears, gathers three hundred eighteen men from his household, chases the kings as far as Dan, attacks by night, and brings everything back: Lot, the people, the goods.
Now Abram is the hero, holding all of Sodom's wealth.
The king of Sodom comes out to meet him with an offer that sounds generous: give me the people, and keep the goods for yourself.

teach.h: NOT A THREAD NOR A SHOE-LATCHET.
teach.b: Abram answers that he has lifted up his hand to God, Maker of heaven and earth, "that I will not take a thread nor a shoe-latchet nor aught that is thine, lest thou shouldest say: I have made Abram rich."
Not even a sandal strap. Why so absolute? He says it himself: so no one can say Sodom made him rich.
Sodom, a city the Torah has already called wicked. Abram doesn't want his fortune tied to that name. His blessing comes from God, or not at all.
And he isn't stingy with others. He sets aside what his young men have eaten, and says his allies, Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, should take their portion. His own principle doesn't cost anyone else.
The Talmud adds a lovely twist.

teach.h: A THREAD AND A STRAP, GIVEN BACK.
teach.b: Because Abram refused a thread and a strap, it says, his descendants were given a thread and a strap: the blue thread of the tzitzit, the fringes, and the strap of the tefillin, from earlier on this path.
The thread he wouldn't take from Sodom comes back to his children as a mitzvah.

how: Jewish ethical teaching points to Abram's refusal of Sodom's spoils as a model of integrity, and the Talmud links it to the mitzvot of tzitzit and tefillin.

o: the spoils of war Abram brought back
go forth, the portion of Abram's journey
the walk to Haran with Terah's family

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: Abram's allies, who take their portion

s: Abram kept the spoils, as the custom was
he refused even a thread or a shoe-latchet.
Abram's refusal cost his fighting men their share
he set aside what his young men had eaten, and his allies took their portion.
the Talmud links the thread and strap to tzitzit and tefillin
because he refused them, it says, his descendants received them.

games.q: you're Abram. you've rescued Sodom's people and goods. the king says: give me the people, keep the goods. what do you say?
o: not a thread nor a shoe-latchet.
games.why: Abram refuses everything, so no one can say Sodom made him rich. but his allies still take their portion.

practice: Look honestly at this week: is there anything, even something tiny, that you took or kept but didn't really earn? Credit, a perk, a borrowed thing never returned, a benefit from someone you don't respect.
Don't beat yourself up; just notice it, then imagine setting it down, and how light your hands feel.

wordCard.voice: Lech Lecha. The portion where Abram rescues his nephew, then refuses Sodom's wealth: not even a thread or a sandal strap.

carryVoice: Your line: not even a thread. A fortune left on the table, and clean hands. See you tomorrow.
